chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
title: Claude Thornhill as a person and afterwards
summary: She calls Claude a quiet genius; after their relationship ended she didn't see him for years.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Yes. You say he didn't have much of a sense of, he didn't have much of a business sense?
Well, I don't think so. I don't think he was interested from that standpoint. You know, he was an artist. You know how it is with us artist. We know absolutely nothing about money.
How else would you describe him? What else would you say about him as a person at this
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

Well, I really think Claude was more of a genius. He was quiet. He had a very droll sense of humor. He wasn't very talkative. He played and arranged and I'm pretty sure that the only thing he thought about is music. From that standpoint, yeah.
You'd say he was a very optimistic kind of a person at that time?
I don't know whether he was optimistic or not. He went along, you know, with not very much to say, just working.
Okay. I guess I asked that because later on after the failure in the 1950's . . .

After our relationship ended I didn't see Claude for years in the '40s. This was, I suppose after the war. / And Claude happened to stroll in there one night and he sat at the piano and played a thing that we had done earlier, "A Brown Bird Singing". I think he was still in uniform. Well, I did see him once after that. After the war was over and his band was together we worked in Chicago. I was on the bill with him in Chicago. And that was the last I saw of

Claude. I didn't keep up with him and he didn't keep up with me.
